newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Kuwait to complete utility privatisation in 2002.
newsitem.headline: Kuwait to complete utility privatisation in 2002.

text.p: Kuwait hopes to start this year the controversial privatisation of public utilities, possibly with the participation of global giants, to complete it by 2002, a senior official said on Tuesday.

"The draft law (for the second phase of the privatisation programme) has been sent to parliament and is on the agenda for the first year which ends in July," the head of the state Kuwait Investment Authority (KIA) Ali al-Badr told Reuters.
"If the law is passed by parliament this year we can complete the privatisation of basic services companies in five years," he said in an interview.

The draft law deals with basic services like health care, power, water and ground telephones. It proposes several solutions to ease MP concerns over the future of Kuwaitis working in these sectors and the price for services once privatised.
It also envisages foreign partnership of 25-30 percent to gain state-of-the-art know-how and efficient management skills.

But unlike the first phase of the programme, to be completed by the end of 1998, KIA will not solely lead the privatisation of public utilities but a yet to be formed higher committee will oversee the complex process.
The committee "will evaluate the assets, devise management systems, decide on pricing for services, come up with the best solutions for the labour issue...," Badr added.
Badr said KIA had sold state stakes in 22 listed and unlisted firms since the launch of the first phase of the privatisation programme in September 1994 for 740 million dinars.
"KIA shares in 11 yet to be privatised main companies, firms which we own more than 25 percent in, and a few minor holdings are worth another one billion dinars," he added.

That does not include closed firms which are also earmarked for privatisation like public transport and Kuwait Airways Corp. A working group is due to come up with a formula for the privatisation of the national flag carrier by August.

Currently all public services are subsidised while these companies are used as employment centres for Kuwaitis. The state employees some 92 percent of Kuwaitis in the work force and provides them with high salaries and generous benefits compared to foreigners of the same grade working in Kuwait.
Some of the Kuwaiti workers "could be made redundant and offered early pension schemes, a compensation of three or four years of salary or retrained to take up another job.
"The government could also offer to pay half of the salary of a Kuwaiti for a few years if the privatised company keeps him on," Badr said of the various options.

Also the price of services could be contained "by paying back to Kuwaitis, not all subscribers, the difference in price, offering the privatised utility a discount on crude used to fire up a power plant for example or introducing a bracket system so moderate users continue to pay low prices," he added.
